text:
Federal court litigation is often viewed as a last resort in U.S. immigration law. For applicants navigating employment-based petitions, particularly under the EB-1A and EB-2 National Interest Waiver (NIW) categories, the prospect of suing the government can seem daunting.

Recent developments, including a widely discussed federal court decision in Mukherji v. Miller, have renewed interest in litigation as a way to challenge denials and delays. But how much do federal court challenges actually affect pending employment-based cases? And what are the tradeoffs to keep in mind before deciding whether to sue?

The answer is nuanced. Litigation can be impactful in certain contexts, but its practical effect depends on the type of claim, the arguments raised, and the broader judicial landscape. Still, when used strategically, litigation can be a powerful tool for correcting agency error and moving cases forward.

What Federal Courts Can (and Cannot) Do in Immigration Cases

A common misconception among applicants is that federal courts can simply “re-decide” an immigration case. In reality, judicial review is much narrower.

In employment-based immigration cases, federal judges generally do not reweigh evidence or substitute their judgment for that of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). Instead, they often ask whether the agency’s decision was arbitrary or capricious (meaning unreasonable or not properly explained), contrary to law, or an abuse of discretion (meaning USCIS acted outside the limits of its authority).

That distinction matters because it affects what a court can actually review. It means that most litigation does not turn on whether an application should have been approved, but rather on whether USCIS followed the correct legal framework and adequately explained its reasoning.

As a result, federal court challenges tend to be most effective when they target systemic or procedural flaws, rather than disagreements over how evidence was evaluated.

Why Some Cases Have Broader Impact: The “Framework” Argument

Occasionally, a case emerges that shifts how attorneys think about litigation. The recent Mukherji decision from the District of Nebraska is one such example.

Rather than focusing only on the applicant’s qualifications, the court scrutinized the two-step adjudicatory framework used in EB-1A petitions—specifically, the interaction between the regulatory criteria and the separate final merits determination, where USCIS evaluates the overall strength of the petition. The court questioned whether this structure had been properly adopted and whether it aligned with governing law.

The court’s ruling was notable because it was directed at more than a single evidentiary dispute. Instead of asking whether USCIS had evaluated one applicant’s evidence correctly, it asked whether the agency was applying the proper legal framework at all.

When courts engage at this level, their reasoning can have implications beyond the immediate case, encouraging attorneys to bring similar claims and prompting broader scrutiny of agency practices.

At the same time, the decision should be kept in perspective. A district court ruling does not create binding precedent nationwide. Even within the same district, other judges are not required to follow it, and an appeals court can still overturn or narrow the decision.

In other words, while cases like Mukherji can influence strategy and generate momentum, they do not automatically change outcomes for all pending petitions.

EB-1A vs. EB-2 NIW: Different Litigation Realities

Not all employment-based categories are equally suited for federal litigation. The distinction between EB-1A and EB-2 NIW cases is particularly important.

EB-1A: More Room for Legal Challenges

EB-1A petitions, which require demonstrating extraordinary ability, are structured around defined regulatory criteria. USCIS’s own guidance provides that, at the threshold stage, officers determine whether the evidence “objectively meets” the regulatory criteria, before proceeding to a separate final merits determination. As a result, challenges at this stage are more likely to center on whether USCIS correctly applied the regulatory criteria, rather than on the kind of discretionary judgment often associated with the final merits determination.

For this reason, EB-1A denials have historically been more amenable to federal court challenges. The Mukherji decision has further bolstered this perception by suggesting that aspects of the adjudicatory framework itself may be open to scrutiny.

EB-2 NIW: A Higher Barrier to Litigation

By contrast, EB-2 NIW cases can present a steeper challenge in federal court when the denial rests primarily on USCIS’s discretionary judgments rather than a clear legal or procedural error.

The EB-2 NIW framework, particularly the inquiries into whether the proposed endeavor has “national importance” and whether the applicant is “well positioned” to advance it, affords adjudicating officers substantial room to assess the factual record. Courts are thus often reluctant to second-guess those judgments absent a meaningful legal error.

That dynamic means EB-2 NIW litigation is often most viable not when the dispute is simply about how persuasive the evidence is, but when the agency applies the wrong standard, ignores key parts of the record, or treats similar evidence inconsistently.

So, while EB-2 NIW cases can be more difficult to litigate successfully, they are not beyond review. The strongest cases are those that identify a concrete legal or procedural defect, rather than merely inviting a court to reweigh the evidence.

The Ripple Effect of Federal Court Decisions

Even when a court decision is not binding, it can still shape the broader legal landscape. A favorable decision can influence later cases as attorneys cite its reasoning, and patterns of analysis start to emerge across different jurisdictions.

This cumulative effect can make certain arguments easier to advance, particularly when multiple courts begin to question the same agency practices.

This process, however, takes time. A single decision rarely transforms the landscape overnight. Instead, its influence depends on whether other courts adopt similar reasoning and whether appellate courts affirm, narrow, or reject the underlying analysis.

Litigation That Directly Affects Pending Cases

While many federal court challenges focus on denials, some forms of litigation have a more immediate and direct impact on pending applications.

Mandamus Actions: Addressing Delays

One of the most common tools is a mandamus action, which is a lawsuit that asks a court to compel the agency to make a decision on a long-delayed case.

These lawsuits do not seek approval of the petition itself. Instead, they argue that the agency has unreasonably delayed or effectively refused to make a decision. That argument is not limited to immigrant petitions, but also arises in nonimmigrant worker petitions such as L-1, O-1, or H-1B, where agency delays can disrupt time-sensitive employment, status, and business needs.

For applicants facing extended processing times, mandamus actions can be an effective way to move a case forward.

Preliminary Injunctions: Freezing the Status Quo

In certain situations, attorneys may seek a preliminary injunction, which temporarily halts government action while the court reviews the case.

In the employment-based context, this is less common for individual petitions but can be highly relevant in broader policy disputes, particularly where delays or restrictions affect the ability to work or maintain status.

Programmatic Litigation: Challenging Policy-Level Actions

The most far-reaching impact on pending cases often comes from programmatic litigation, where plaintiffs challenge a government policy affecting large groups of applicants.

Recent examples include challenges to pauses or restrictions affecting immigrant visas, adjustment of status (AOS), employment authorization documents (EADs), and other related benefits. In these cases, litigation can influence not just one petition, but entire categories of pending applications.

Choosing the Right Cases for Federal Litigation

Despite growing interest in federal litigation, it is not a one-size-fits-all solution, and pursuing it requires careful judgment. The most successful cases are typically those that are supported by strong factual records that highlight inconsistencies, involve issues that go beyond simple disagreement over evidence, and arise in favorable jurisdictional contexts.

Even in well-positioned cases, outcomes can vary. Courts may defer to the agency, decline jurisdiction, or interpret the law differently than anticipated. For this reason, effective litigation is not just about filing a lawsuit, but about identifying the right case, the right arguments, and the right timing.

For law firms, this also means aligning litigation strategy with broader case goals and client expectations. A thoughtful, selective approach is essential, not only to maximize the likelihood of success, but to ensure that litigation genuinely advances the client’s long-term immigration strategy.

Frequently Asked Questions About Federal Court Immigration Cases

Can you sue USCIS after a denial?

Yes, in some cases. A federal court can review whether USCIS followed the law, but it will not re-evaluate your evidence.

What is a mandamus lawsuit in immigration?

A mandamus action asks a court to compel the agency to make a decision on an unreasonably delayed case.

Will filing a lawsuit lead to USCIS approving my case?

In most cases, a federal court does not approve the petition itself, nor will it compel the agency to issue an approval. Instead, it reviews whether the agency followed the law, applied the correct legal framework, and adequately explained its decision. If the court finds a legal defect, the usual remedy is to set aside the decision and remand the matter to the agency for further proceedings consistent with the court’s ruling. In delay cases, the court may order the agency to make a decision, not dictate the outcome.

Will filing a lawsuit hurt my case?

It should not prejudice the outcome in your case. USCIS’s adjudication of a case and a federal court’s review of agency action operate in different spheres and should proceed independently. Filing suit does not change the legal standard USCIS is supposed to apply or give the agency a lawful basis to deny relief. But it can affect timing, which is why the decision to sue should still be made strategically.

Conclusion: An Effective Tool in the Right Case

Federal court challenges can play an important role in employment-based immigration cases involving legal error, unreasonable delay, or broader agency practices. At the same time, not every case is well suited for litigation, especially where decisions rest heavily on agency discretion. The key is understanding when litigation is the right tool, and when other avenues may be more effective.

For applicants, the takeaway is not that litigation guarantees success, but that it can be a powerful option in the right circumstances. With a clear strategy and a deep understanding of how courts approach these cases, federal litigation can serve as an important pathway to challenge improper decisions and move cases forward.

title: Social media users critical of immigration crackdown targeted by DHS subpoenas
description:
Through his attorneys, the Reddit user on Friday declined to comment on the current state of his case.
However, when asked by media outlets, including NewsNation, for data that would substantiate those claims, DHS has failed to respond.
Google’s most recent Transparency Report indicated that it received nearly 61,000 requests for user information between January and June of 2025, 28,622 of which came from federal subpoenas.
Trujilo added that social platforms should do more to protect users beyond alerting them when they have been targeted.
“They could easily step up and fight back against these subpoenas on their users’ behalf, and so far, they haven’t been doing that.
text:
(NewsNation) — The Department of Homeland Security has been filing administrative subpoenas with popular social media platforms for several months now, demanding otherwise protected personal information of users it insists have been critical of the agency, especially in social posts involving federal immigration enforcement operations around the United States.

The federal agency’s efforts to publicly identify certain posters are raising concerns among First Amendment advocates and civil liberties organizations, which argue the federal government is violating the users’ constitutional right to free speech by seeking to unmask their true identity.

‘Lawless’: Social media user information handed over to federal government

Big Tech companies like Google, Meta and Reddit have received subpoenas demanding that social media users’ names, email and IP addresses, along with other basic information, be handed over to the federal government, according to the Electronic Frontier Foundation. In many cases, the tech companies have complied unless the users legally challenge the government’s order, Mario Trujillo, an attorney with the EFF, told NewsNation.

Yet with many Americans unable to afford private legal representation, federal officials are gaining access to their personal information based almost solely on certain users’ social media messaging, Trujilo said, calling the filing of the subpoenas “lawless.”

“These investigations, these subpoenas, they all feel very centered around harassment over speech that the government doesn’t like,” Trujillo said. “What these people are doing is protected First Amendment speech, and that is unquestioned.”

He added, “It’s hard to understand what the (government’s) motivation is. I think the administration is trying to chill speech, and this is one way they’re going about it.”

Reddit user targeted after posting about ICE officer who fatally shot Renee Good

Most recently, DHS officials have threatened to bring a Reddit user from the Pacific Northwest before a federal grand jury in Washington, D.C., over comments he posted about Jonathan Ross, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who fatally shot Renee Good in Minneapolis in January.

The man, referred to as “John Doe” in court filings, was originally the target of an administrative summons filed on behalf of a Virginia ICE officer who was mentioned in the Reddit post. The Oregon-based Civil Liberties Defense Center filed a motion to quash the summons, which the government subsequently withdrew, as has been the case in the majority of subpoenas filed by DHS.

But 12 days later, Reddit received a grand jury subpoena from the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Washington, D.C., in connection with the same user’s Reddit post. Reddit has until April 21 to respond, but Lauren Regan, the director of litigation and advocacy at CLDC, told NewsNation this week that her organization would file a motion to quash the grand jury summons, which it did Friday.

In a statement released by his attorneys in late March, “John Doe” said he was “alarmed and fearful” to receive word from Reddit that the government had requested his personal information. He described the quashing of the original subpoena by lawyers as “a major relief.”

“This is not just a win for one person but for anyone who speaks out against government abuses,” he said.

Through his attorneys, the Reddit user on Friday declined to comment on the current state of his case.

CLDC previously represented a client who was behind the website Stopice.net and was targeted by DHS for posts on Meta. After CLDC filed a motion to quash that legal action, the feds withdrew their subpoena and have not gone after the user since, Regan said.

In both cases, the speech used by both clients did not come close to crossing a line that would be considered criminal behavior, Regan said. In the most recent DHS allegation, “John Doe” reposted publicly known information about Good’s shooter and added a line that said he hoped the ICE officer’s next location was a state prison, she added.

“It is just criticism (of DHS) on a public forum,” Regan told NewsNation this week. “That just really begs the question that the goal by targeting just kind of normal citizens who are participating in these forums, the idea is to censor and scare everyone into thinking if they criticize the government or immigration enforcement, they, too, may have their privacy invaded and their First Amendment rights threatened.”

Immigration officers facing spike in assaults, Homeland Security claims

In a statement to NewsNation, DHS said any allegations the agency attempted to squash free speech are “categorically false.”

In the case of “John Doe,” the agency said the issuing of the administrative subpoena was part of an investigation into threats and doxxed ICE officers who are “experiencing coordinated campaigns of violence against them.”

In its response, DHS indicated federal immigration officers and agents are facing a 1,300% increase in assaults, a 3,200% increase in vehicular attacks and an 8,000% increase in death threats.

However, when asked by media outlets, including NewsNation, for data that would substantiate those claims, DHS has failed to respond. Regan referred to the statistics as DHS “propaganda that has no basis in fact.”

However, by threatening a grand jury against the latest “John Doe,” Regan said DHS is taking “it up a notch” by involving what Regan called a “secret tribunal.” The purpose of calling a federal grand jury is to investigate a federal crime, which Regan says her client has not committed, and that by pursuing a grand jury indictment, the Trump administration is instead ramping up attacks on free speech.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for Washington, D.C., did not respond to NewsNation’s request for comment on the pending case.

Regan and Trujillo believe the pattern of threatening those who criticize federal actions follows a familiar script from the Trump White House.

“What we have seen by and large is that often, this administration attempts to do something that is unlawful, and if nobody challenges it, they get away with it,” Regan said.

Social media subpoenas increase

According to Reddit’s Transparency Report for the first six months of 2025, the company received 1,179 government and law enforcement agency requests for account information, a 12% increase from the previous six-month period.

Of those, 777 of the requests came from the U.S. government or police agencies. Reddit said it disclosed data in 640 (82%) of the U.S. cases.

A total of 423 of the inquiries seeking information came from U.S. subpoenas, and another 27 came from court orders, the report indicated.

A Reddit spokesperson told NewsNation that “privacy is central to how Reddit operates.” The company’s newest transparency report is due out within the next few weeks, the spokesperson said.

“We do not voluntarily share information with any government, especially not on users exercising their rights to criticize the government or plan a protest,” the spokesperson told NewsNation.

The company said that when it does disclose data, it only provides “the minimum required” and contacts the Reddit user whose information is being sought, “so they can defend their interests.” Reddit’s chief legal officer wrote in a post on the platform that users who are the targets of administrative subpoenas are notified by the company before any information is disclosed to the government.

Like Reddit, Google publishes a transparency report that provides the general public with information about the types of requests the company receives. The company says it is “standard policy” to notify Google users when they are the target of federal subpoenas, court orders or warrants in order to give them a chance to take action.

The only case users are not informed, the company said, is when it is legally prohibited from doing so.

Google’s most recent Transparency Report indicated that it received nearly 61,000 requests for user information between January and June of 2025, 28,622 of which came from federal subpoenas. It turned over information in 89% of those cases.

“Our processes for handling law enforcement requests are designed to protect users’ privacy while meeting our legal obligations,” a Google spokesperson told NewsNation. “We review all legal demands for legal validity, and we push back against those that are overbroad, including objecting to some entirely.”

How threats of federal legal action are curbing Americans’ social media posts

The two civil rights attorneys told NewsNation that as federal agencies like DHS go after those who criticize its actions, the use of fear and intimidation is prompting some to reconsider what they post, even behind usernames that don’t reveal their true identities.

“I do think the (government’s) intention is to scare people into submission and scare people from publicly sharing their disdain or their distrust or criticism of the government,” Regan said. “And the regime will be somewhat successful in that. There will be people who choose not to say certain things online because they don’t want to end up in this boat.”

What agencies like DHS are doing with a user’s information once they have it remains unclear, Trujillo said. In cases like the Reddit user who could face a grand jury in Washington, the government may be trying to build a criminal case against the user, which creates another legal hurdle to clear in proving clear criminal intent.

“(The challenges) are showing DHS, ‘What’s the point of continuing to do this?’ These subpoenas are invalid; they’re going to be quashed. Why continue to do this?” EFF’s Trujillo told NewsNation. “I’m not sure (DHS officials) are rational actors and (that the challenges) are going to make them stop. I think it would make a rational actor stop, but hopefully, it has some sort of effect on them.”

Social media companies should ‘fight back’ against subpoenas: Attorney

In the majority of cases, the social media companies receiving administrative subpoenas have not filed motions to quash them, placing the onus on the social media posters themselves to challenge the government’s invasion of privacy, attorneys told NewsNation.

With Reddit and Google’s compliance rate with government subpoenas both over 82% in 2025, attorneys suggest that tech companies will continue to hand user information over to the feds. Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, did not respond to a NewsNation request for comment about subpoenas it has received.

Both civil liberties attorneys who spoke to NewsNation argued that, in most cases, high-tech companies do not want to place themselves in legal jeopardy of being accused of being in contempt of a government order, which prompts them not to fight the subpoenas they receive.

That has prompted some users, like the Reddit user “John Doe,” to fight back despite mounting legal bills that, in some cases, could reach tens of thousands of dollars if a private attorney is needed.

Trujillo said that organizations like EFF, the ACLU and CLDC handle cases pro bono but that under the Trump administration, these groups’ resources have been stretched thin. Trujilo added that social platforms should do more to protect users beyond alerting them when they have been targeted.

“These tech companies are bankrolled by billions and billions of dollars, (and) they have armies of lawyers,” he told NewsNation. “They could easily step up and fight back against these subpoenas on their users’ behalf, and so far, they haven’t been doing that. I think that’s a thing they should be urged to do.”

text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (KOIN) — Six months after several Oregon lawmakers asked the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw federal agents deployed to Portland, they’ve finally received a response.

In a letter dated April 15, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement acting director Todd Lyons outlines the circumstances that led to the deployment of federal agents to Portland, otherwise known as “Operation Black Rose.”

The operation began on Sept. 27, 2025 and lasted through March 1, according to the letter. It included approximately 100 ICE personnel, which included officers and agents from ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations and ICE Homeland Security Investigations. Partner agencies such as U.S. Customs and Border Protection, the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives also participated.

“Such large-scale operations would be less necessary if sanctuary jurisdictions, like Portland, Oregon, cooperated with ICE and other federal law enforcement agencies in the execution of their statutory responsibilities,” Lyons wrote.

Oregon lawmakers originally reached out to express concern of the widespread use of tear gas and its impact on the neighboring community—an issue that has been extensively reported and has since become the subject of multiple lawsuits. They also had concerns about ICE agents wearing masks to conceal their identities and reports that some were not clearly identifying themselves in interactions with community members.

Lyons’ letter said that ICE agents only use force when no other option is available and that when possible, they coordinate with local officials when using chemical irritants such as tear gas. He also said that some ICE agents may wear masks for their personal safety but are required to identify themselves as immigration officers.

“This so-called response after six months to our delegation letter is both late and lame in its failed defense of Donald Trump and Kristi Noem’s needless and inflammatory deployment of masked agents to Portland,” said U.S. Senator Ron Wyden, D-Ore.

“The vast majority of Oregonians protesting ICE abuses peacefully exercised their First Amendment rights, and I’ll never stop advocating for them or opposing these Trump policies that treat the Constitution like a doormat,” he added.

text:
This story is republished with permission from KFF Health News.

As immigration authorities carry out what President Donald Trump has promised will be the largest mass deportation operation in U.S. history, several states are passing laws to keep children out of foster care when their detained parents have no family or friends available to take temporary custody of them.

The federal government doesn't track how many children have entered foster care because of immigration enforcement actions, leaving it unclear how often it happens. In Oregon, as of February two children had been placed in foster care after being separated from their parents in immigration detention cases, according to Jake Sunderland, a spokesperson for the Oregon Department of Human Services.

"Before fall 2025, this simply had never happened before," Sunderland said.

As of mid-February, nearly 70,000 people were being held by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The record 73,000 people in detention in January represented an 84 percent increase compared with one year before. According to reporting from ProPublica, parents of 11,000 children who are U.S. citizens were detained from the beginning of Trump's term through August.

The news outlet NOTUS reported in February that at least 32 children of detained or deported parents had been placed in foster care in seven states.

Sandy Santana, executive director of Children's Rights, a legal advocacy organization, said he thinks the actual number is much higher.

"That, to us, seems really, really low," he said.

Separation from a parent is deeply traumatic for children and can lead to various health and psychological issues, including post-traumatic stress disorder. Prolonged, intense stress can lead to more-frequent infections in children and developmental issues. That "toxic stress" is also associated with damage to areas of the brain responsible for learning and memory, according to KFF.

Maryland, New York, Washington, D.C., and Virginia amended existing laws during Trump's first term to allow guardians to be granted temporary parental rights for immigration enforcement reasons. Now the enforcement surge that began after Trump returned to office last year has prompted a new wave of state responses.

In New Jersey, lawmakers are considering a bill to amend a state law that allows parents to nominate standby, or temporary, guardians in the cases of death, incapacity, or debilitation. The bill would add separation due to federal immigration enforcement as another allowable reason.

Nevada and California passed laws last year to protect families separated by immigration enforcement actions. California's law, called the Family Preparedness Plan Act, allows parents to nominate guardians and share custodial rights, instead of having them suspended, while they're detained. They regain their full parental rights if they are released and are able to reunite with their children.

There are significant legal barriers to reunification once a child is placed in state custody, said Juan Guzman, director of children's court and guardianship at the Alliance for Children's Rights, a legal advocacy organization in Los Angeles.

If a parent's child is placed in foster care and the parent cannot participate in required court proceedings because they are in detention or have been deported, it's less likely they will be able to reunite with their child, Guzman said.

An estimated 5.6 million children are U.S. citizens who live with a parent or family member who does not have legal immigration status, according to research from the Brookings Institution, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank. Within that group, 2.6 million children have two parents lacking legal status.

Santana said he expects the number of family separation cases to grow as the Trump administration continues its immigration enforcement campaign, putting more children at risk of being placed in foster care.

ICE directives require the agency to make efforts to facilitate detained parents' participation in family court, child welfare, or guardianship proceedings, but Santana said it's uncertain whether ICE is complying with those rules.

ICE officials did not respond to requests for comment for this report.

Before the change in California's law, the only way a parent could share custodial rights with another guardian was if the parent was terminally ill, Guzman said.

If parents create a preparedness plan and identify an individual to assume guardianship of their children, the state child welfare agency can begin the process of placing the children with that individual without opening a formal foster care case, he added.

While Nevada lawmakers expanded an existing guardianship law last year to include immigration enforcement, the measure requires the parents to take the additional step of filing notarized paperwork with the secretary of state's office, said Cristian Gonzalez-Perez, an attorney at Make the Road Nevada, a nonprofit that provides resources to immigrant communities.

Gonzalez-Perez said some immigrants are still hesitant to fill out government forms, out of fear that ICE might access their information and target them. He reassures community members that the state forms are secure and can be accessed only by hospitals and courts.

The Trump administration has taken unprecedented steps to access sensitive information through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, the IRS, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, the Department of Housing and Urban Development, and other entities.

Gonzalez-Perez and Guzman said that not enough immigrant parents know their rights. Nominating a temporary guardian and creating a plan for their families is one way they can prevent feelings of helplessness, Gonzalez-Perez said.

"Folks don't want to talk about it, right?" Guzman said. "The parent having to speak to a child about the possibility of separation, it's scary. It's not something anybody wants to do."

text:
PROVIDENCE, R.I. (AP) — A federal judge on Friday dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit demanding detailed voter data from Rhode Island, a decision that follows similar rulings in a handful of other states.

U.S. District Court Judge Mary McElroy sided with Rhode Island's top election officials and civil rights advocates, writing that federal law does not permit the U.S. Department of Justice "to conduct the kind of fishing expedition it seeks here."

READ MORE: Judge sides with Arizona election official in ruling that could affect midterms voting

In an emailed response, the Justice Department said it would not comment on ongoing litigation.

McElroy's decision is similar to other rejections by federal judges across country since the Justice Department began seeking detailed voter data from the states. The information includes dates of birth, addresses, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers.

Federal officials say they need the voter data to ensure election security, but Democratic and some Republican officials have objected to the requests and said such a demand violates state and federal privacy laws.

"The executive branch seems to have no problem taking actions that are clear Constitutional overreaches, regularly meddling in responsibilities that are the rights of the states," Rhode Island Secretary of State Gregg M. Amore said in a statement. "But the power of our democratic republic, built on three, coequal branches of government, is clearer than ever before."

Some election officials have raised concerns that federal officials will use the sensitive data for other purposes, such as searching for potential noncitizens. Those concerns were raised again after the DOJ's attorneys acknowledged in the Rhode Island case that the department was seeking unredacted voter roll information so it could be shared with the Department of Homeland Security to check citizenship status.

At least 12 states have either provided or promised to provide their detailed voter registration lists to the department, according to the Brennan Center: Alaska, Arkansas, Indiana, Louisiana, Mississippi, Nebraska, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas and Wyoming.

Meanwhile, the DOJ has sued at least 30 states and the District of Columbia seeking to force release of the data. In addition to Rhode Island, judges have rejected those attempts in California, Massachusetts, Michigan and Oregon. In Georgia, a judge dismissed a DOJ lawsuit because it had been filed in the wrong city, prompting the government to refile elsewhere.

In Rhode Island, McElroy sided with the federal judge's decision in Oregon. That ruling said the federal government was not entitled to unredacted voter registration lists containing sensitive data and said the Justice Department had failed to identify a basis or a purpose for requesting the voter records.

"Absent from the demand are any factual allegations suggesting that Rhode Island may be violating the list maintenance requirements," McElroy wrote.

text:
Only have a minute? Listen instead

Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

It’s a story that has become all too familiar.

An individual, a Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipient, without a criminal history, who has seemingly done everything that the United States government has asked of them, was arrested, detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents for months before a perplexed judge ordered his release.

Brenda Peña and her family found themselves in the midst of one such scenario when her husband of four years, Jahasiel Peña Enriquez, was arrested and detained by ICE agents as he drove to work on the morning of Jan. 29.

He’d worked as an equipment operator in the oil fields, but he’d recently opened his own business doing body work for high-end vehicles.

As per their usual routine, he’d helped his wife get their two oldest children ready for school, a 7-year-old boy and a 5-year-old girl. The couple also have a 3-year-old son.

While Brenda drove the children to school, her husband drove to his shop in Donna, a drive of approximately four or five minutes.

“I had just dropped off my kids, and he called me. He’s like, ‘Hey, I’m getting stopped by an undercover cop. Just come over here, just to be on the lookout’,” she recalled.

Shortly afterward, she received a text message from Jahasiel.

“He’s like, ‘It’s ICE’,” she recalled. “Right then and there, my heart just dropped. I was in shock. Honestly, I was hoping it was like a joke or something, but once he called me back because they allowed him to give me a call to notify me that they’re taking him, he called me and he told me, ‘Hey, they’re taking me in.’”

The agents told Jahasiel that they had a warrant for his arrest.

Jahasiel, who was born in Tamaulipas, had lived in the United States since 2000 when he was 5 years old. He’d been a DACA recipient since 2013. At the time of his arrest, his DACA status was in the process of being renewed.

Brenda immediately drove to the location where her husband was being arrested. When she arrived, she took out her phone and began recording the situation.

“As soon as I got there, I recorded because I know that this is something that would be good to have for the attorney so he can listen to what the ICE agents stated,” she said. “When I got there, the ICE agent came up to me, and he told me that the reason why they were detaining him was because they saw he was renewing (his DACA) and that he had no legal status.

“According to them, their arrest was going to make the process faster for him. I’m not sure for what, but I mean, all that information they gave me is false.”

The video was shared with MyRGV.com. In the video, Brenda can be seen approaching ICE agents near a silver-colored SUV.

An agent wearing a black tactical vest with patches that read POLICE and ICE approached Brenda.

“Why is he being detained?” she asked him.

“The reason we arrested him is because he just recently applied for a authorization document, so he has no legal status right now,” the agent explained.

Jahasiel had applied to renew his DACA status in Nov. 2025. His application was still pending at the time of the arrest, but his status was not going to expire until Feb. 13.

“So what’s going to happen — he’s going to go see a judge, OK? And the judge will decide if he has some type of benefits,” the agent continued. “He’s actually going to expedite the process, OK? So you don’t have to worry about it. He might get a chance to bond out, but he has to go through the proceedings before the judge.”

The ICE agent can be heard telling Brenda that she can speak with her husband briefly before he is taken to their office in Edinburg. He explained that he would be able to call her once he got there.

“He is going to be detained, and, like I said, he’s not going to be deported or anything like that,” the agent can be heard telling Brenda.

“That’s what you guys say,” Brenda is heard saying as she begins to cry.

“He’s gotta go see the judge, and like I said, he might have a chance to bond out,” the agent said.

“He’s never done anything bad,” Benda said.

“He has no status. That’s the thing,” the agent replied.

“Yes, but we already applied,” she pleaded.

“I’ve already explained, OK,” the agent said, visibly frustrated.

Later, she was allowed to approach Jahasiel, who’s seen handcuffed in the front passenger seat of the vehicle.

He is heard making arrangements for his vehicle to be picked up and asking if his wife can take his wallet and his phone. He then kisses his wife goodbye before she is seen walking back to her car.

“I was frantic in that moment,” Brenda recalled. “I was crying, and I was out of words. I didn’t really know what to say, and I wish I could have said more and spoke out more, but my attorney mentioned to me how it wouldn’t have made a difference. These agents don’t care, and they just would have taken him anyways.”

Jahasiel was transported to the Edinburg ICE facility before being sent to the Webb County Detention Center in Laredo.

“I just felt a lot for my kids and for him, because I know it was difficult,” Brenda said. “He’s never been handcuffed, and he went through a lot of trauma in processing. They just had him in handcuffs, like for hours and hours and hours, and it was traumatic to him.”

“This guy did everything, right,” Ricardo Ramirez, an Edinburg-based attorney who represents Jahasiel, said. “I mean, he had everything to the tee. He had a long-term plan to be in the United States with his wife as a permanent resident. But just from one second to the next, everything gets cut down. And unfortunately, I mean, there’s nothing else this guy could have done.”

While Jahasiel’s case is one that many DACA recipients are experiencing. But unlike many who have been detained at the hands of ICE since President Donald Trump’s second term began, Jahasiel has been granted a new opportunity.

He was released from the detention facility on April 1, and has since returned home to his family. Now, with his DACA approved and extended, he is working to become a legal permanent resident.

“It’s just mind boggling how this guy did everything right, and yet, still he was detained, deprived of liberty for a couple of months,” Ramirez said. “I mean, the judge even said whenever we had his final hearing, ‘I don’t even know why they’re detaining you guys.’ She was perplexed as well.’”

As for Brenda, she said that she and her family are just happy to have Jahasiel back home. She said that they are now trying to pick up the pieces from his detainment.

“He’s been doing good. I mean, he’s happy he’s home and stuff, but, you know, he’s experiencing like PTSD from that traumatic experience,” Brenda said. “He’s very cautious now when we’re driving. Certain vehicles give him some kind of anxiety.”

“It’s something that I hope doesn’t last long with him, but it’s something that he’s dealing with right now,” she continued. “Overall he’s been good. I mean, I’m happy, and my children are happy to get back to their normal routine.”

text:
Only have a minute? Listen instead

Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

Nine days after his detention by federal immigration agents, Dr. Ezequiel Véliz, a second-year UTRGV family medicine resident at Knapp Medical Center in Weslaco, was released to his husband’s custody Wednesday, ending an ordeal that supporters and civil rights advocates say is yet another example of wrongful detention by government agencies.

Prior to his release, his husband, Joseph Williams, said in an interview with MyRGV.com this week that Ezequiel told him of sickness that spread throughout the facility where he was being held — the Rio Grande Detention Center in Laredo — and cases of detainees being pressured to sign self-deportation documents without explanation.

Joseph said the ordeal began when traveling to Houston and despite Ezequiel having the correct documentation and no criminal history.

We the People RGV, a partisan political organization in the Valley, called his detention a violation of due process in a news release announcing Ezequiel’s release after being granted bond.

“We need accountability for why this happened and safeguards to prevent future due process violations,” We the People RGV said in their statement.

Similar sentiments were shared with the organization by political candidates that included physicians such as Dr. Ricardo Villarreal and Dr. Ada Cavazos Cuellar.

South Texas Equality Project President Hector Ruiz also told the organization on Wednesday that Véliz “is a compassionate physician and beloved member of our community. We are overjoyed he is being reunited with his husband today.”

HOW IT ALL STARTED

On Monday, April 6, Ezequiel was on his way to Houston with Joseph when things took a turn for the worse. When the couple approached the Sarita checkpoint, Joseph told officers that he was a U.S. citizen and his husband was pending a work visa.

After showing agents documentation supporting Ezequiel’s pending work visa, the couple was asked to pull over and Ezequiel was taken inside for questioning.

Joseph waited for two hours before hearing anything about his husband’s situation, during that time agents asked him to move his vehicle further up to not block agents’ vehicles from passing.

A female officer explained to Joseph that they were working on corroborating the paperwork that Ezequiel had presented to officers.

The process was taking longer because they needed lawyers to look into Ezequiel’s case because officers can only check if a visa is expired or current and can’t look at what has been filed or pending.

After four hours of waiting, Ezequiel finally returned to the vehicle to tell Joseph he was being detained due to agents claiming he allegedly overstayed his travel visa in 2018.

He had returned to the vehicle to grab a box filled with paperwork from their vehicle; however, officers did not allow him to bring the documents with him.

Joseph explained that Ezequiel told officers that the documents were proof of his legal presence in the country.

Agents continued to deny his request and only allowed him to bring a couple of things.

“I don’t want to be here. I’m really scared,” Joseph recalled Ezequiel saying as officers took him away.

At that moment Joseph attempted to call Ezequiel’s friend Genesis, who had been waiting to hear back from him about his situation.

During that time Joseph was approached by two Border Patrol agents who told him he can’t be parked in that area. Although he had explained to the agents that he was directed to that spot earlier and just wanted to make a quick phone call, officers were still asking him to move his vehicle.

Joseph said he had been given conflicting instructions from two agents on where to go, and when he decided on driving nearby a white billboard as per one agent, another agent he described as being “rude” accosted him for not following his instructions instead.

“Do you have a problem? Do you not understand English? I said go to the rest area. What don’t you f-ing understand? Are you stupid?” Joseph recalled that officer yelling.

Joseph explained that he was getting conflicting instructions, but was told, “‘I don’t care what he said, I’m telling you, go to the rest area, go! Move this truck unless you want to have a problem. Do you want to have a problem?’”

Joseph, adding that the agent began to bang his hands on the side of the U-Haul as he continued to yell at him, said he drove off in fear just praying he’d get to Houston soon.

“It was awful,” Joseph said in a low tone. “It was a very traumatic experience.”

EZEQUIEL’S VISAS

In 2018, Ezequiel, a native of Venezuela, visited the United States with a tourist visa.

With the help of a lawyer, Ezequiel filed for an extension of the visa to visit some of the universities in the area.

Despite the extensions being granted, agents are now claiming Ezequiel overstayed his visa during that time.

Joseph explained that Ezequiel had receipts in a box of documents proving the extension process in 2018.

After returning home Ezequiel decided he wanted to continue his medical education in the U.S. and applied for a student visa.

When the COVID-19 pandemic hit in 2020, the university he was attending closed its doors at the facility Ezequiel was at and moved the school to the university’s home location in New York City.

By that point Ezequiel had already applied for the temporary protective status, or TPS, and enrolled in a different school in Houston.

Through the TPS he also received a work permit.

After completing his medical education in Houston, Ezequiel matched with UT Health at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley Family Medicine Residency Program at Knapp Medical Center in Weslaco.

Ezequiel was in his second year of residency when the Trump administration announced that Venezuela no longer met the criteria for TPS, which in his case meant it would be expiring in November 2025.

During that time he returned to his university in Houston to get his school visa documentation with the hopes of converting the visa into a work visa

With support from the university, Ezequiel applied for a J-1 visa in October 2025.

A J-1 visa allows for exchange visitor programs for non-immigrants in the U.S., which includes receiving graduate medical education or training according to the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

This type of visa requires individuals to have a designated sponsor, DS-160 form and a DS-2019 form.

On Nov. 17, 2025, Ezequiel’s TPS status expired and was told by the school they could no longer employ him legally and had to let him go.

However, his work visa was still valid and the school assisted Ezequiel in asking for an extension, which was granted for another month and is valid until June 30.

“He’s been waiting for six months now for them to just approve the work visa but status is still pending,” Joseph said.

LIFE IN THE CENTER

Over the last couple days prior to his release Joseph has been able to talk to Ezequiel, who was detained at the Rio Grande Detention Center in Laredo, via phone call.

Although the newly wed couple is devastated to be apart, Joseph explained that he gets some peace of mind every time he is able to talk with Ezequiel.

“It is nice that I get to see his face,” Joseph said Monday, adding that Ezequiel was permitted his own tablet to be able to contact his family.

During those talks, Ezequiel has expressed concerns for the treatment of detainees in the center.

“He described it as like an H-E-B … with no aisles with food in it. It’s just a giant warehouse with bunk beds,” Joseph said. “There’s hundreds of people in here, it’s not ideal.”

He added that Ezequiel described the environment as chaotic with many detainees yelling.

Ezequiel also explained that he’s one of many detainees who’s sick with a cold and cough, which is spreading in the facility.

Joseph has reached out to congressmen including U.S. Rep. Vincent Gonzalez, D-Brownsville, for help to release Ezequiel.

He hoped Gonzalez could reach out to the Department of Homeland Security to inquire about the delay in response for Ezequiel’s work visa. Joseph hopes the congressman can help push for an emergency junction for Ezequiel so they can get the work visa through the system.

“He’s a community services person,” Joseph said. “This isn’t fair … he hasn’t done anything wrong, he’s not a criminal and they treat him like a criminal.”

The Trump administration, ICE and DHS have made the case that agencies are only targeting immigrants who are in the country illegally and who have criminal records; however, as much as 70% of ICE detainees have no U.S. criminal conviction, an independent analysis by Transactional Records Clearinghouse has found.

Ezequiel also explained to Joseph that officers have detainees sign documents without explanation of what the form is for.

An officer attempted to have Ezequiel sign something without him reading the contents of the paper telling him that “it’s just a formality,” Joseph said.

He added that Ezequiel read the documents anyway and refused to sign it when he realized one document was asking him if he would like to self deport and the other document was stating he was agreeing to isolate himself while in custody.

For Ezequiel it felt as if officers were using the language barrier to get detainees to either self deport or self isolate. He encouraged other detainees to not sign the papers.

“… Some of these people are probably self deporting and not even realizing that they’re giving up all their rights because they’re signing away their rights to due process’,” Joseph recalled Ezequiel saying.

text:
A police chief from Gratis, Ohio, questioned Cincinnati school officials about immigrant students.

The chief, Tonina Lamanna, told the district's lawyer she was working for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Lamanna was previously fired from the Dayton Police Department in 2017 amid accusations of being untruthful.

Since 2018, she has worked for four different Ohio police departments before becoming chief in Gratis.

Police Chief Tonina Lamanna traveled 50 miles from her police station in the small town of Gratis, Ohio, walked into a Cincinnati public school around lunchtime and started asking questions about immigrant students.

After being turned away from three schools on April 15, Lamanna later told the school district's lawyer that she was doing work for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, general counsel Dan Hoying said. ICE confirmed local law enforcement partners were conducting "welfare checks" on children who arrived in the country unaccompanied during President Joe Biden's administration.

The incident sparked outrage in the district with a school board member calling Lamanna "a puppet of ICE."

But who is Lamanna?

She became the chief of the Gratis Police Department in August 2024, according to an article from the Register-Herald in Eaton. She previously was the assistant police chief for the village of about 850 people.

At that time, the Register-Herald reported that Lamanna also ran a business as a dog groomer and trainer, taught at Butler Tech and volunteered for a local fire department with a dog used to investigate arson cases. The article states she had extensive training in handling police dogs, numerous certifications and a master's degree in education.

Her career started in 1999 when she joined the Verona Police Department, northwest of Dayton, according to state records. By 2001, she was working at the Dayton Police Department.

Lamanna rose through ranks to become a sergeant in Dayton, but was then fired from that department in 2017 on accusations she was untruthful and filed false documents, according to a report from the Dayton Daily News.

She was fired in the midst of a gender discrimination lawsuit she had filed against the department. In 2018, Dayton's Civil Service Board upheld the firing. She lost the discrimination lawsuit in federal court and the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected her appeal in 2019.

She was hired in 2018 as a part-time officer by the Union City Police Department near the Ohio-Indiana border. Then in 2020, she was hired as an auxiliary officer in Harveysburg.

Since her time in Dayton, she has worked for four different Ohio police departments, according to state records.

From 2021 to 2023, she worked at the Camden Police Department, then in November 2023 joined the Gratis Police Department as a part-time officer, according to state records. She became a full-time officer there in 2024 when she was promoted to chief.

After the incident in Cincinnati, Gratis councilwoman Vicki Blankenship told The Enquirer that she trusts that Lamanna would not be doing anything she should not be.

"She built our police department up with pennies," Blankenship said. "We're just a small town. She's doing all the right things."

Butler County Sheriff Richard K. Jones, whose department also has agreements with ICE, said Lamanna should have stayed in her jurisdiction.

“She never should have done it,” Jones told Enquirer media partner Fox 19. “She never should have gone out of her jurisdiction and surely shouldn’t have gone to Hamilton County or the city.”

The Enquirer has left multiple message for Lamanna since the April 15 incident and has not received a reply.

text:
Welcome to POLITICO’s West Wing Playbook: Remaking Government, your guide to Donald Trump’s unprecedented overhaul of the federal government — the key decisions, the critical characters and the power dynamics that are upending Washington and beyond.

Send tips | Subscribe | Email Sophia | Email Ben

FIRST IN WEST WING PLAYBOOK: White House chief of staff SUSIE WILES and JAMES BLAIR are convening dozens of Republican political consultants from across the country at the Waldorf Astoria in Washington on Monday, according to a person familiar with the plan and granted anonymity to describe it. The gathering comes as the White House and its allies intensify preparations for a challenging midterm cycle and is aimed at sharing data and strategy as well as aligning operatives on how best to support candidates, the person said.

The Waldorf meeting — on the heels of President DONALD TRUMP’s announcement that Blair would temporarily step down as deputy chief of staff to lead the president’s political operation — reflects a new phase of coordination between the White House and the broader Republican political apparatus, with a clear eye toward holding the House and the Senate — the latter increasingly viewed by some allies as being more realistic.

The meeting follows an earlier strategy session in February at the Capitol Hill Club, where Wiles, Blair and other top Trump political advisers huddled with Cabinet officials on how to sharpen the GOP’s midterm messaging and better sell Trump’s agenda.

Taken together, the sessions underscore growing urgency inside the White House about the midterms and concerns around energy prices and cost of living exacerbated by the Iran war.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

YOU’RE GOOD TO GO: A Cambodian national convicted of aggravated robbery in 1993. A stateless Palestinian man who pleaded guilty to driving under the influence and drug crimes in 2018. A Ukrainian man who fled the war with Russia in 2022 only to lose lawful status last year when he accidentally drove his Uber Eats delivery across the Mexican border. A Cuban man convicted of child abuse in 2020.

All four had previously been ordered deported from the U.S. and were arrested by ICE in recent months. But all four were ordered released by federal judges appointed by Trump who concluded that their detentions violated constitutional limits. They are among hundreds of immigrants targeted amid the Trump administration’s mass deportation drive with murky histories — and sometimes sordid criminal records — who nevertheless have been found by federal courts to be illegally detained.

ICE’s drive to lock up thousands of undocumented immigrants with no criminal records and yearslong ties to the U.S. has ignited a political and legal backlash to the Trump administration’s unprecedented policy of mass detention. But federal judges have routinely found that this second population — immigrants, including some with criminal records, who have been issued final deportation orders yet remain in the country — have faced similar abuses of due process and violations of constitutional rights.

A POLITICO analysis of immigration detention cases has found that federal judges have ordered bond hearings and, more often, outright release for more than 400 people detained under these circumstances. And the rebukes have come from judges appointed by every president since RONALD REAGAN.

“President Trump always prioritizes the safety and wellbeing of the American people. Certain activist judges, however, have purposefully sought to promote the interests of dangerous criminal aliens whom they have ordered released into American communities to victimize the public with impunity,” said White House spokesperson ABIGAIL JACKSON. “This Administration will stop at nothing to uphold the rule of law, and protect our country from these dangerous illegal aliens.”

At issue is a complex aspect of immigration law that governs the treatment of people issued “final orders of removal” by immigration courts. In some cases, those final orders were issued decades ago but could not be carried out because the country on the other end of the order — China, Russia, Cuba, Syria, Iran — has strained relations with the U.S. or generally resists accepting deportees. In other cases, the immigrants are stateless, born in a now-obsolete Soviet Union or lacking ties to any country. And in yet another category, immigration judges have credited deportees’ fears of persecution or torture and granted them protections from being sent to their home countries.

U.S. District Judge JOHN HINDERAKER, a Trump appointee in Arizona, ordered the release of a Cameroonian woman who was ordered deported but protected from being sent to her home country over concerns about torture. U.S. District Judge DOMINIC LANZA, another Arizona-based Trump appointee, recently ordered the release of a Honduran woman, convicted of sex crimes in 2006 and incarcerated until 2022, who received similar protections from torture in her home country.

The Supreme Court has agreed that people in this category can be detained for roughly six months without constitutional concerns — a period in which ICE is expected to arrange their deportations by securing travel documents and scheduling flights. But once that period elapses, a constitutional presumption for liberty kicks in.

In some cases, the Justice Department claims in court that the administration has renewed efforts to arrange long-stalled deportations, reigniting conversations with reluctant countries or finding alternate “third countries” willing to accept deportees. The Trump administration has partnered with African countries to receive some deportees who can’t be sent to their home countries, for example. But here, too, judges say the administration is often supplying wishful thinking rather than concrete evidence of progress.

“The Government offers no documents, no diplomatic agreements, and no concrete evidence. … Instead, the Government extends hope and a placeholder,” U.S. District Judge KYLE DUDEK, a Trump appointee, said in a recent order releasing a Cuban man from immigration custody, despite the administration’s efforts to send him to Mexico. “A mere representation from an agency to its lawyers — unbacked by a shred of evidence — cannot justify keeping a man locked in a cell.”

Have you picked up on any upcoming moves or policy changes? We want to hear from you on how this is playing out. Email us at westwingtips@politico.com.

POTUS PUZZLER

Which president was obsessed with mastodons?

(Answer at bottom.)

Agenda Setting

HORMUZ OPEN (AGAIN): The Strait of Hormuz, the waterway crucial for global trade that Iran has effectively closed since the beginning of the U.S.-Iran conflict, has reopened after a 10-day ceasefire was called between Israel and Lebanon, Trump and a top Iranian official said this morning, our FINYA SWAI, ELI STOKOLS and JACK DETSCH report. Trump welcomed Iran’s reopening of the strait, declaring the critical waterway “COMPLETELY OPEN AND READY FOR BUSINESS” but said that a U.S. naval blockade there remains in effect for Iranian ships.

Trump, in a social media post, said he’d lift that blockade only after “OUR TRANSACTION WITH IRAN IS 100% COMPLETE,” expressing optimism that negotiations on a broader deal with Tehran “SHOULD GO VERY QUICKLY.”

In a second post, Trump claimed that the U.S. will “get all nuclear dust” out of Iran in an agreement, the details of which remained unclear. The president’s declaration aimed to settle markets amid a rise in oil prices and growing concerns about the global economic impact of a prolonged impasse in the strait. His blockade of ships heading to and from Iranian ports, which began this week, is an effort to negate Iran’s main point of leverage in negotiations over the future of its nuclear program.

STILL … The Iran war is risking America’s global security ties and damaging its reputation, especially among the world’s Muslims, according to a set of State Department cables obtained by our NAHAL TOOSI. The cables, dated Wednesday, described the fallout of the war for America’s standing in three countries in different parts of the world: Bahrain, Azerbaijan and Indonesia. U.S. diplomats at embassies in the countries’ capitals painted damning portraits of an America under siege in multiple media spheres by pro-Iranian actors that are exceptionally agile in the digital space.

The cables carry veiled requests for the Trump administration to free up American embassies to fight such negative narratives online and in traditional media.

The Oval

MORE ON IRAN: Following Trump’s announcement that Iran has reopened the strait, Trump told NewsNation that Iran had agreed to “everything,” including that it would stop enriching uranium. In a separate call with Reuters this afternoon, the president said that the U.S. will work with Iran to recover its enriched uranium and bring it back to the U.S. “We’re going to get ‌it together. We’re going to go in with Iran, at a nice leisurely pace, and go down and start excavating with big machinery. ... We’ll bring it back to the United States,” Trump said.

And in an interview with Axios, the president said U.S. and Iranian negotiators will likely meet this weekend, where he expects a deal to come to fruition to end the war “in the next day or two.”

“The Iranians want to meet,” Trump said. “They want to make a deal.”

TOURIST SEASON: Anthropic CEO DARIO AMODEI is expected to meet with top White House officials today as anxiety grows across Washington over the cybersecurity risks posed by the company’s new AI model Mythos, our BRENDAN BORDELON, CHEYENNE HASLETT, JOHN SAKELLARIADIS and GABBY MILLER report. Amodei is expected to meet with Wiles and other Trump administration officials, according to three people familiar with the plans, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive conversations.

One of the people said Treasury Secretary SCOTT BESSENT will also be in attendance. The meeting comes less than two months after the White House and Defense Department declared Anthropic a risk to the country’s national security supply chain, objecting to the company’s insistence on limiting its software use for mass surveillance or autonomous weapons.

According to an email sent to federal agencies and obtained by POLITICO, the Office of Management and Budget is now mulling whether agencies will be allowed to use a “modified” version of Mythos.

DAMAGE CONTROL: After a week of Trump depicting himself as JESUS CHRIST in an AI-generated meme and attacking POPE LEO XIV as “WEAK on Crime,” the White House faith office hit the airwaves this morning. In an interview with Real America’s Voice, White House faith office director PAULA WHITE-CAIN said the president can “quote so many sermons. I mean, profound.”

White-Cain, who has been Trump’s spiritual adviser for decades, said the president has “always had faith in his life,” pointing to his 2024 assassination attempt as a moment when “POTUS recognized that God saved him. … That was the real … awakening day.”

What We're Reading

She Made Sure Her Baby Was Born an American. Then Federal Agents Separated Them. (NYT’s Caroline Kitchener, Charo Henríquez and Hamed Aleaziz)

That would be THOMAS JEFFERSON. Jefferson ordered mastodon bones to be brought back from the largest fossil site in North America at the time. Once procured, Jefferson and a colleague spread the bones across the floor of a room inside the White House to catalog them, in hopes of completing the first full mastodon skeleton — and to select specimens to send to France to counter French scientist COMTE de BUFFON’s theory that American animals were inferior to European ones.
